question: In what year did Brenvale Ceramics open its first export warehouse in Port Ashby?
document: Brenvale Ceramics traces its origins to a single wood-fired kiln behind a farmhouse outside Corran Falls. The company was founded in 1962 by Ottilie Brenvale, a former schoolteacher who had taught herself glazing from library books. For its first decade the firm sold mostly to restaurants and hotels within a day's drive, building a reputation for heavy stoneware that survived commercial dishwashers. Growth accelerated when Brenvale's son, Marius, joined the business and pushed for sales beyond the region. Fourteen years after the company's founding, Brenvale Ceramics opened its first export warehouse in Port Ashby, giving it direct access to shipping lines serving northern Europe. The warehouse handled fewer than forty pallets in its first month but soon became the busiest part of the operation. Today the company employs more than three hundred people across two production sites and still fires a limited line of tableware in a restored version of Ottilie's original kiln. In a statement marking the release of its new spring catalogue, chief executive Hanna Brenvale-Ostrow said the firm remains 'a family company that happens to ship to thirty countries.'

Fourteen years after the company's founding, Brenvale Ceramics opened its first export warehouse in Port Ashby, giving it direct access to shipping lines serving northern Europe.

question: How many workers in total are employed at Quillmont Logistics' three regional distribution centers?
document: HALDEN JUNCTION — Quillmont Logistics today announced the completion of a two-year modernization program across its regional distribution network. The company, which provides warehousing and last-mile delivery for grocery and pharmacy chains, operates three regional distribution centers. The Halden Junction facility, the oldest of the three, employs 412 workers and handles the bulk of the company's chilled freight. The Brookfast center employs 268 workers and specializes in pharmaceutical storage under temperature-controlled conditions. The newest site, in Ashcombe Vale, employs 175 workers and opened with fully automated sorting lines. The modernization program replaced conveyor systems at all three sites and introduced a shared inventory platform that allows stock to be rebalanced between centers overnight. 'Our people made this transition possible while keeping trucks on the road every single day,' said chief operating officer Delphine Marsh. Quillmont said it expects the upgrades to reduce average order processing times by roughly a fifth. The company does not plan to open a fourth distribution center before the end of the decade, but it intends to expand its delivery fleet next spring.

The Brookfast center employs 268 workers and specializes in pharmaceutical storage under temperature-controlled conditions.
The newest site, in Ashcombe Vale, employs 175 workers and opened with fully automated sorting lines.

document: Pascovane Instruments has spent six decades building precision balances for laboratories, pharmacies and assay offices. Its founder, Lionel Pascovane, grew up in the river town of Drellingham, where his father repaired clocks. In 1954 he joined Corlett Optical as an apprentice lens grinder, and he later moved into the firm's small scale-calibration department. After eleven years at Corlett Optical, Pascovane left to found his own company, convinced that the balances used in hospital laboratories were neither accurate nor durable enough. His first product, the Model A analytical balance, was assembled in a rented garage and sold to a single university chemistry department. Word spread quickly, and within a few years the company had moved into a purpose-built workshop on the edge of town. Pascovane Instruments now sells its products in more than forty countries and employs roughly five hundred people. The company announced this week that it will open a new calibration laboratory dedicated to pharmaceutical customers, which it describes as a return to the founder's original mission of making measurement trustworthy.

Dr. Varga-Holm completed her doctorate under Professor Anselm Rudd, whose work on heat-stable enzymes laid the groundwork for several of Tessaline's current assays. 'Ines has spent her career making enzymes behave in the field the way they behave in the lab,' he said. document: Pellandine Insurance today announced that its board has named Tobias Wren as the company's next chairman, succeeding Rosalind Achterberg, who will retire from the board at the end of the year. She joined the company's claims department as a graduate trainee and rose through underwriting and finance before being appointed chief executive in 2003. question: By how many barrels did Gorsemoor Brewing Company's annual output increase between its first full year of operation and 2021?
document: Gorsemoor Brewing Company began in a converted dairy barn on the moorland edge of Fallowby, where three friends pooled their savings to buy secondhand fermentation tanks. The brewery's first beer, a dark mild called Peat Lantern, remains its best seller. In its first full year of operation, Gorsemoor brewed 6,250 barrels, nearly all of it sold to pubs within twenty miles of the barn. Demand grew steadily as the brewery added a pale ale and a seasonal porter, and in 2014 it relocated to a larger site on the Fallowby industrial estate. In 2021, Gorsemoor brewed 19,000 barrels, a record for the company despite disruption to the hospitality trade. The company announced today that it will invest in a canning line to supply supermarkets for the first time, a move that co-founder Elspeth Rainey described as overdue. 'We held out for a long time because we wanted to be a pub brewery,' Rainey said. 'But people want to drink our beer at home too, and we would rather they find it on a shelf than not at all.' The canning line is expected to be operational by late spring.

question: How many new stores did Tamberly Hardware open during its 2023 expansion?
document: Tamberly Hardware today reported the results of its 2023 expansion program, the largest in the retailer's forty-year history. The family-owned chain, known for its staffed tool-rental counters and Saturday repair workshops, had previously operated only in its home county of Ardwell. During the 2023 expansion, Tamberly opened 12 stores in the Calder Valley region. It also opened 7 stores in the Lowmarsh district, most of them in former supermarket buildings. A further 9 stores opened along the Ferris coast, where the company says demand for marine and garden supplies is strongest. No stores were closed during the year. Managing director Owen Tamberly said the new locations had been chosen to sit within an hour's drive of the company's central warehouse in Ardwell, allowing next-day restocking. 'We did not want to grow faster than our trucks could follow,' he said. The company reported that like-for-like sales in its original stores rose modestly, while the new stores together accounted for roughly a third of fourth-quarter revenue. Tamberly said it has no further openings planned for the coming year.

question: In what month and year did Corvane Robotics begin shipping its original Skylark drone to customers?
document: Corvane Robotics, a maker of agricultural drones, has published a short history of its Skylark series to mark the retirement of the original model. The Skylark was followed by the Skylark Pro, which added a spraying attachment, and by the current Skylark 3. Corvane says more than 4,000 units of the original model remain in active use. question: In what year was Thistlecombe Mills founded?
document: Thistlecombe Mills, the woollen blanket maker based in the Carrow valley, has announced the reopening of its heritage visitor centre after a year-long restoration. The centre first opened in 2011. That year, the company celebrated the hundredth anniversary of its founding. The centre occupies the original dye house, a stone building beside the mill race that powered the company's first looms. The restored centre includes a working hand loom, a collection of pattern books dating back to the mill's earliest decades, and a new gallery devoted to the women who made up most of the weaving workforce in the years after the First World War. Thistlecombe remains independently owned by descendants of its founder, the wool merchant Cecily Harrowgate, and still sources most of its fleece from farms within the valley. Chief executive Robin Harrowgate-Lowe said the restoration was funded partly by sales of the company's limited-edition centenary blanket, which has been reissued for the occasion. The visitor centre will be open daily from Easter until the end of October, with weekend opening during the winter months.

question: How many shares did each founding partner of Dunbarrow & Pryce Engineering receive at incorporation?
document: Dunbarrow & Pryce Engineering, the structural consultancy behind several of the region's best-known footbridges, today announced that it will become employee-owned. The firm was incorporated by three founding partners: structural engineer Alasdair Dunbarrow, geotechnical specialist Miriam Pryce, and the architect-turned-engineer Colm Faraday. At incorporation, the company issued 600,000 shares. The shares were divided equally among the three founding partners, an arrangement that the firm says reflected their determination to run the practice as a partnership of equals. Faraday's name was never added to the company's title, a decision he later described as 'the only argument I was happy to lose.' Under the new arrangement, an employee ownership trust will acquire a controlling stake from the founders' families over the next five years. Managing partner Leonie Pryce, Miriam Pryce's niece, said the move would protect the firm's independence and its culture of mentoring young engineers. The consultancy employs 85 people across offices in Brannock Quay and Ellisford, and it will continue to trade under its existing name.
